    Syllabus

    This syllabus moves from toolchain basics to ownership, then into application design and a tested command-line capstone. Modules 0–1 are available; Module 2 is partially implemented (Topics 1–7 are published, Topic 8 is planned). All other modules below are planned; Module 3 Topics 1–2 are published. Follow the numbered order; later modules name any additional prerequisites. A topic listed here is not necessarily a published lesson.

    0. Hello, Rust and tooling

    • Install Rust and understand rustup, rustc, Cargo, rustfmt, Clippy, and rust-analyzer.
    • Build, run, format, check, test, and package a Hello World application.
    • Optional extensions: Debian packaging, compiler outputs, Cargo workspaces, and Raspberry Pi Pico cross-compilation. These are not prerequisites for Module 1.

    Completion goal: build, run, format, and check a Hello World application.

    1. Rust fundamentals

    All eight topics are published: an overview, bindings, scalar types, collections, functions, conditions, loops, and Cargo/testing practice. Follow the topic index in numbered order.

    • Variables, mutability, scalar and compound types.
    • Functions, expressions, control flow, and pattern basics.
    • Arrays, tuples, String, and Vec<T>; loops, indexing, and basic methods.
    • Structuring small programs with Cargo.
    • Testing simple behavior and reading compiler feedback.

    Completion goal: write and test a function that summarizes a list of numbers.

    2. Ownership and borrowing

    • Values, variables, scope, stack and heap storage.
    • Move semantics, Copy, and Clone.
    • Shared and mutable borrowing.
    • Collections, iterators, slices, and API boundaries.
    • Introductory lifetimes: references must remain valid while used (planned Topic 8).
    • Advanced ownership continues in Modules 8–10 and 13 after structs and traits.
    • Hands-on review: ownership tracing, move repair, snapshots, borrowed iteration, numeric/text slices, and an advanced pipeline combining borrowing with ownership transfer.

    Completion goal: implement functions that read and update caller-owned data without unnecessary clones, and explain a borrow-checker diagnostic.

    3. Structs, enums, and data modeling — Topics 1–2 published

    • Define structs and implement methods with impl blocks.
    • Use associated functions and model domain data.
    • Define enums and use match, if let, and pattern matching.
    • Represent missing values with Option<T>.
    • Model operation outcomes with Result<T, E>.

    Completion goal: model a task with a struct, status enum, and methods, then demonstrate success, a missing task with Option, and a rejected operation with Result.

    4. Traits and generics — planned

    • Define and implement traits.
    • Use generic functions, generic types, and trait bounds.
    • Derive common traits such as Debug, Clone, and Default.
    • Compare trait bounds, impl Trait, and dyn Trait at an introductory level.

    Completion goal: implement one trait for two types and use both through a generic function.

    5. Error handling, modules, and testing — planned

    • Distinguish recoverable errors from panics and interpret Result.
    • Create custom error types and propagate errors with ?.
    • Organize modules, visibility, Cargo targets, and unit/integration tests.
    • Read files and test malformed input and missing files.

    Completion goal: build a library plus binary that loads data and reports errors without using unwrap() for expected failures.

    6. Rust software design and patterns — planned

    • Prerequisites: Modules 3–5.
    • Encapsulation: private fields, validated constructors, and types that prevent invalid states.
    • Apply SOLID pragmatically: focused responsibilities, useful extension points, trait behavioral contracts, small interfaces, and dependency inversion.
    • Compose structs, enums, and traits; inject dependencies through constructors and function parameters.
    • Design public APIs with deliberate ownership, borrowed parameters, meaningful errors, and minimal exposed implementation details.
    • Use Builder, Strategy, Adapter, State, and Newtype patterns when concrete requirements justify them; compare enum-based and trait-based designs.
    • Separate core application logic from CLI input, file storage, networking, and hardware; refactor incrementally with tests.

    Completion goal: build a task service with a small storage trait, an in-memory implementation for tests, and a file implementation. Test the same behavioral contract for both, and explain why each abstraction is needed.

    7. Command-line task tracker capstone — planned

    • Parse command-line commands and arguments.
    • Combine structs, enums, ownership, borrowing, and error handling.
    • Persist tasks to a file using a stable data format.
    • Split the application into focused Cargo modules.
    • Apply Module 6 design principles to separate task logic from CLI and storage.
    • Add unit tests, integration tests, and useful user-facing errors.

    Completion goal: provide add, list, complete, and delete commands; preserve tasks across runs; test valid commands, invalid input, and persistence failures.

    8. Closures and advanced iterators — planned

    • Prerequisites: Modules 2–5.

    Planned topic sequence

    1. Closures and captures: closure syntax, borrowing captures, move, and the Fn, FnMut, and FnOnce traits.
    2. Iterator fundamentals and laziness: Iterator, next(), and why adapters do no work until the iterator is consumed. Apply the same methods to ranges and collection iterators.
    3. Transforming and filtering: map() changes each yielded value; filter() keeps values matching a predicate.
    4. Selecting and numbering: take() limits the number of items, skip() omits initial items, and enumerate() pairs items with zero-based positions. Revisit rev() and step_by() and explore how adapter order changes results.
    5. Consuming results: sum(), count(), and collect(), including the type annotations needed to choose a sum type or output collection.
    6. Ownership through pipelines: compare iter(), iter_mut(), and into_iter() when closures read, change, or take ownership of elements.
    7. Custom iterators and practice: implement Iterator for a small type, then build and test a filtering pipeline with empty and no-match cases.

    Completion goal: build and test a filtering pipeline with a closure whose capture mode you can explain.

    9. Advanced lifetimes and smart pointers — planned

    • Prerequisites: Modules 3–5 and 8.
    • Borrowed structs, lifetime annotations, elision, and method receivers.
    • Ownership in Option and Result; as_ref and as_mut.
    • Box, Rc, and RefCell; interior mutability and ownership design.

    Completion goal: compare owned and borrowed representations, and demonstrate shared ownership with checked interior mutation.

    10. Threads and concurrency — planned

    • Prerequisites: Modules 8–9.
    • Thread spawning, joining, channels, Send, and Sync.
    • Arc, Mutex, and RwLock; lock scope and deadlock avoidance.

    Completion goal: implement a threaded worker example and test that all results are collected and all threads terminate.

    11. Async Rust — planned

    • Prerequisites: Modules 8–10.
    • Futures, async/.await, executors, and task ownership.
    • Async I/O, cancellation, timeouts, and avoiding blocking work in async tasks.

    Completion goal: implement concurrent I/O with explicit timeout and error handling.

    12. Performance and profiling — planned

    • Prerequisites: Modules 7–9; Modules 10–11 for concurrent examples.
    • Release builds, benchmarks, profiling, allocation costs, and cloning costs.
    • Measure changes while preserving behavior and tests.

    Completion goal: benchmark a working program, identify one bottleneck, and compare performance before and after a tested improvement.

    13. Unsafe Rust and FFI — planned

    • Prerequisites: Modules 9–12.
    • Raw pointers, safety contracts, and small safe interfaces around unsafe code.
    • C interoperability, ABI boundaries, and allocation ownership across FFI.
    • Self-referential designs and pinning, revisiting futures from Module 11.

    Completion goal: wrap a small FFI call with documented ownership and safety requirements and tests for its safe interface.
